AMD’s $8.2 Billion AI Bet Comes With a $1 Trillion Valuation Problem
On September 29, Rosenblatt reiterated its Buy rating and $700 price target on Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) after the company announced that it had entered into a definitive agreement to acquire World Labs, an AI model and research lab led by AI pioneer Dr. Fei-Fei Li.
Rosenblatt believes the acquisition could expand AMD's AI software, modeling, and simulation capabilities at a time when the AI market is developing rapidly and increasingly requires system-level expertise beyond traditional semiconductor capabilities. The deal is valued at $8.2 billion in an all-stock transaction and is expected to close by the end of 2026.
The research firm noted that World Labs' engineers could help accelerate AMD's development of AI platforms at the system level while also opening opportunities in new markets such as robotics.
The firm sees the acquisition as bringing forward R&D spending that AMD would otherwise need to undertake to develop this technology in-house. Rosenblatt also approves AMD management's decision to grow the company's AI capabilities.

Acquisition Adds Long-Term Potential, But Some Concerns Remain
The deal comes with some risks for investors. AMD said it will pay the $8.2 billion purchase price in stock. This means that the transaction will dilute existing shareholders. In addition, the acquisition does not immediately translate into chip revenue or earnings, meaning investors will need to wait for the new capabilities to make meaningful contributions.
The transaction also adds execution and integration risk at a time when AMD's valuation already reflects substantial expectations for AI-driven growth. As of October 2, the stock has gained more than 180% year-to-date and the company is now valued at more than $1 trillion.

Management's outlook points to continued momentum. AMD expects Q3 revenue of approximately $13 billion, which represents about 41% year-over-year growth. AMD (AMD +2.95%) has had an incredible year. It's the ninth-best-performing S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.73%) stock, rising nearly 200% so far this year. That performance has pushed it to become a $1 trillion company. While Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%) is still ahead at a $5.5 trillion valuation, is this a sign that AMD is finally catching up?
Let's take a look at both of these stocks and see if Nvidia investors have something to be worried about or if AMD has maximized its short-term returns.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Both companies are competing for market share in the AI arms race. They are primarily doing this in the graphics processing unit (GPU) sector, but there are also countless other companies that operate in data centers, which are major market opportunities. Nvidia took an early lead in 2023 because its products were flat-out better than AMD's. Nvidia had leading GPUs and software to program them, so it naturally took a huge lead to start.

AMD is looking to close the gap and has released several promising GPUs alongside improving its programming software to compete with Nvidia's CUDA. This is driving strong growth for AMD, as its data center revenue rose 107% year over year to $6.7 billion in the second quarter. Companywide, AMD's revenue rose 50% to $11.5 billion. That's a pretty strong performance from AMD, but the problem is, Nvidia's is better.
Nvidia is both bigger and growing faster. In its data center division, it delivered 117% year-over-year growth to $89 billion. Nvidia has less exposure to consumer and original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) demand, so its overall growth rate was also faster, rising 106% to $96.2 billion.

Nvidia is growing faster and has a data center division that's well over 10 times AMD's. However, AMD is about a fifth the size of Nvidia, so what's going on here?
I think this is a telling sign, as the market is highly valuing AMD's stock while downplaying Nvidia's. This could be a huge investment opportunity, and those who made a huge return on AMD stock can roll it into Nvidia's for a huge gain in 2027.
AMD's stock is very expensive compared to Nvidia's
Not all of AMD's stock success is genuine. Some of it has come from its business performance improving, but much of it has come from its valuation rising, which puts the stock on unstable ground. AMD trades at a very expensive 158 times trailing earnings and 81 times 2026 estimates. Even when 2027 projections are used, AMD's stock trades at nearly 40 times forward earnings.
AMD PE Ratio data by YCharts.
Now, let's contrast that with Nvidia's price tag. Nvidia trades for less than 30 times trailing earnings. That's right, Nvidia's trailing earnings are less than AMD's price tag when next year's earnings projections are used.
NVDA PE Ratio data by YCharts.
That's a huge gap, and it shows just how expensive AMD's stock is and how cheap Nvidia's is. When next year's forward earnings are used for Nvidia, it trades at a mere 14.7 times forward earnings. If Nvidia and AMD should trade for about 30 times trailing earnings, then AMD investors could expect about a 25% downside next year, while Nvidia investors would expect their stock to double.
Nvidia represents a compelling investment opportunity, while AMD is standing on a shaky foundation. AMD is still growing slower and smaller than Nvidia and hasn't done anything to take market share from Nvidia quite yet. However, the market has priced AMD's stock like it's already won the battle. This mismatch won't last forever, and I think Nvidia will be a far better stock to own as the market figures out what's going on with these two.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is creating a major opportunity in the central processing unit (CPU) market, positioning Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) for robust growth.
Bank of America strategists expect the server market to expand from approximately $61 billion to $211 billion by 2030. The firm estimates that roughly $180 billion of the $211 billion server CPU market in 2030 will be tied to AI workloads, creating a significant market for AMD’s EPYC server processors.
AMD also ranks among Insider Monkey’s 11 AI Stocks That Will Go to the Moon— but where does it rank among the other AI names on the list?
On September 25, the research firm reiterated a Buy rating on AMD. It raised its price target to $720 from $620, citing the company’s opportunity to capture a larger share of the rapidly expanding CPU market.
AMD’s rally has already pushed expectations sharply higher, raising a tougher question: what does a $1 trillion valuation now demand from AMD’s AI ambitions?
Agentic AI Could Boost Demand for AMD CPUs
BofA’s higher price target comes as the firm expects agentic AI to increase demand for CPUs that coordinate workloads, manage data, and support increasingly complex AI systems.
Rather than replacing GPUs, CPUs are increasingly complementing them within AI infrastructure. This trend is already supporting AMD’s CPU business.
The price target hike comes as BofA expects agentic AI to fuel demand for CPUs to coordinate workloads and manage data. CPUs increasingly complementing GPUs rather than competing with them drove growth in AMD CPU revenue in Q2. Client business revenue was up 23% year over year to $3.1 billion, driven by strong demand for Ryzen processors.
Additionally, Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. is well positioned to gain from AI infrastructure beyond GPUs. The company offers a wide range of platforms that combine EPYC CPUs with Instinct GPUs and networking technologies. That was one reason the company’s data center revenue rose 107% in the second quarter to $6.72 billion, driven by growth in EPYC server CPUs and Instinct GPUs.
AMD’s AI Opportunity Extends Beyond GPUs
BofA’s bullish view does not depend on Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. replacing Nvidia as the dominant provider of AI accelerators. Instead, the firm sees AMD as a potential beneficiary of the broader evolution of AI computing architecture.
As AI workloads become more complex and increasingly autonomous, data centers require CPUs, GPUs, networking, and other components to work together efficiently. This creates an opportunity for AMD to benefit from the overall expansion in AI infrastructure, even if GPUs remain the primary engines for many AI workloads.
The opportunity surrounding CPUs could become particularly important as agentic AI applications require greater coordination between different computing resources.
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.’s rapid expansion in AI has also raised expectations for the stock. The stock has gained more than 180% in 2026, reflecting investor optimism about the company’s ability to capture a larger portion of the AI infrastructure market.
The stock trades at a premium, with a forward price-to-earnings multiple of 39X, roughly two times Nvidia’s 19X. This means investors are paying considerably more for each dollar of AMD’s expected future earnings.
Nevertheless, robust growth from a smaller base justifies AMD’s valuation, as second-quarter revenue was up 50% while data center revenue more than doubled year over year. On the other hand, Nvidia boasts of a profitability advantage, as its gross margins stand at about 75% compared to AMD’s 54%.
Any signs that AI infrastructure spending is slowing, or that AMD is capturing less of the expected CPU opportunity, could pressure investor sentiment. A significant portion of expected growth is also tied to hyperscalers, AI labs, and data-center infrastructure providers. If these customers reduce or delay capital expenditures, the company could experience a meaningful slowdown in growth.
Institutional investors have also been increasing their exposure to AMD amid the AI boom. As of the second quarter, 164 hedge funds held positions in AMD, up from 134 in the first quarter, indicating increased institutional participation.
Among individual investors, Marshall Wace LLP increased its AMD position by 3% to approximately $2.26 billion, while DE Shaw reduced its exposure by 21% to approximately $1.79 billion.
Short interest, meanwhile, remained relatively modest. AMD had approximately 39.98 million shares sold short as of September 15, down from 41.71 million shares on August 31. That represented approximately 2.46% of the float. That represented short interest of approximately 2.45%.
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.’s investment story is increasingly tied to the broader AI computing ecosystem rather than GPUs alone. BofA’s $720 price target reflects the firm’s view that the rapid growth of AI workloads could create a substantial opportunity for AMD’s EPYC CPUs alongside its Instinct GPUs and networking products.
The key question for investors is whether the company can continue translating the enormous growth in AI infrastructure spending into sustained CPU and data-center revenue growth. With expectations already elevated following the stock’s substantial rally, execution, hyperscaler spending, and the pace of AI adoption will remain important factors for AMD shares.

AMD stock currently hovers around $616, reflecting a remarkable 187% gain since January and a staggering 281% appreciation over the trailing twelve months. The semiconductor manufacturer momentarily achieved the prestigious $1 trillion valuation milestone on September 21, 2026, before settling slightly lower.
During his September 28 Mad Money broadcast, Jim Cramer weighed in on the extraordinary performance. He characterized Lisa Su’s corporate transformation as “potentially the greatest turnaround in business history” and expressed confidence that momentum remains intact.
Su assumed the chief executive position on October 8, 2014. At that juncture, shares traded near $3 and the entire enterprise commanded a mere $2.5 billion market capitalization.
Cramer’s Focus: Central Processing Units Over Graphics Accelerators
Cramer’s bullish perspective on Advanced Micro Devices doesn’t center on graphics processing technology. Instead, he’s concentrating on central processing units and the emerging paradigm of agentic artificial intelligence.
Agentic AI architectures possess the capability to analyze situations, formulate strategies, and execute decisions autonomously. These computational workflows emphasize inference operations that run continuously, creating demand profiles that favor CPUs over the training-centric GPU requirements that propelled Nvidia’s dominance.
AMD’s EPYC server processor lineup has steadily captured market share from Intel over recent years. Data center segment revenue reached $6.7 billion during Q2 2026, representing a 107% year-over-year increase.
The chipmaker’s sixth-generation EPYC processors debuted in July, engineered specifically to handle agentic computing workloads. Additionally, AMD finalized an $8.2 billion acquisition of World Labs, a research organization established by Dr. Fei-Fei Li, significantly enhancing its internal artificial intelligence capabilities.
Understanding the $1 Trillion Valuation Achievement
While Nvidia’s data center division alone generated $89 billion in revenue last quarter—exceeding AMD’s total by more than thirteen times—Nvidia’s $5.5 trillion valuation represents only approximately five times AMD’s market capitalization.
This valuation differential reveals that market participants aren’t evaluating AMD based solely on current performance metrics. Instead, investors are betting on the company’s future trajectory.
Cramer acknowledged an important qualification. Any security that climbs 30% within a single month and temporarily touches a $1 trillion valuation faces considerable risk of profit-taking should unexpected developments emerge.
Nevertheless, he maintained his optimistic outlook. Su has negotiated commitments from Anthropic for up to 2 gigawatts of MI450 GPU capacity and broadened AMD Helios installations with industry leaders including Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle.
Among 36 Wall Street analysts who published research on AMD during the past three months, 30 recommend buying the stock. Notably, zero analysts rate it a sell, according to TipRanks data.
On Wednesday, September 30, shares edged down 0.59% notwithstanding the introduction of Ross, a sophisticated AI assistant engineered to accelerate engineering workflows spanning design, testing, debugging, and software development.
Ross leverages an extensive AMD knowledge repository containing technical documentation and implementation guides. The platform also employs reusable “agent skills” that enable teams to replicate successful methodologies across multiple initiatives.
“The AMD Ross agentic AI assistant has been a valuable addition to our development workflow,” said Geetha Govindaraj of iWave Global. AMD plans to add new tools to Ross each month.
The minor price decline occurred despite several analyst firms publishing updated research on Tuesday, September 29. William Blair’s Sebastien Naji maintained a Hold stance without establishing a price objective, StoneX’s Cody Acree reiterated a Buy recommendation at $685, and Stifel’s Ruben Roy affirmed a Buy rating at $635.
The Street’s aggregate assessment of AMD stands at Strong Buy, derived from 30 Buy recommendations and six Hold ratings issued during the previous three months. The consensus price target of $648.07 suggests approximately 7% appreciation potential from present trading levels.

A headline-driven surge in interest can fade quickly, whereas sustained customer activity tends to provide a better foundation for planning capacity, staffing and capital allocation. Beyond the headline figures, the pattern of repeat activity often says more than a single strong period, since durable demand tends to hold up across multiple cycles rather than fading once initial attention moves elsewhere. How Plant Focus Shapes Results?

How Overall Logic Holds Together?

Companies often face pressure to pursue fast-growing themes, yet the most durable outcomes usually depend on maintaining service quality, customer retention and operational control in the existing franchise. Overextending into new areas at the expense of the core business can create strain, even if the new opportunity looks attractive on paper in the near term.

No. Market conditions provide context, but the more durable assessment depends on company-specific demand, execution, customer relationships and operating milestones.

Is Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) Still a Buy After Its 180% Plus Rally?
The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is creating a major opportunity in the central processing unit (CPU) market, positioning Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) for robust growth.
Bank of America strategists expect the server market to expand from approximately $61 billion to $211 billion by 2030. The firm estimates that roughly $180 billion of the $211 billion server CPU market in 2030 will be tied to AI workloads, creating a significant market for AMD's EPYC server processors.
AMD also ranks among Insider Monkey's 11 AI Stocks That Will Go to the Moon— but where does it rank among the other AI names on the list?
On September 25, the research firm reiterated a Buy rating on AMD. It raised its price target to $720 from $620, citing the company's opportunity to capture a larger share of the rapidly expanding CPU market.

Posonskyi Andrey/Shutterstock.comAMD's rally has already pushed expectations sharply higher, raising a tougher question: what does a $1 trillion valuation now demand from AMD's AI ambitions?
Agentic AI Could Boost Demand for AMD CPUs
BofA's higher price target comes as the firm expects agentic AI to increase demand for CPUs that coordinate workloads, manage data, and support increasingly complex AI systems.
Rather than replacing GPUs, CPUs are increasingly complementing them within AI infrastructure. This trend is already supporting AMD's CPU business.
The price target hike comes as BofA expects agentic AI to fuel demand for CPUs to coordinate workloads and manage data. CPUs increasingly complementing GPUs rather than competing with them drove growth in AMD CPU revenue in Q2. Additionally, Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) is well positioned to gain from AI infrastructure beyond GPUs. The company offers a wide range of platforms that combine EPYC CPUs with Instinct GPUs and networking technologies. That was one reason the company's data center revenue rose 107% in the second quarter to $6.72 billion, driven by growth in EPYC server CPUs and Instinct GPUs.
AMD's AI Opportunity Extends Beyond GPUs
BofA's bullish view does not depend on Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) replacing Nvidia as the dominant provider of AI accelerators. Instead, the firm sees AMD as a potential beneficiary of the broader evolution of AI computing architecture.
As AI workloads become more complex and increasingly autonomous, data centers require CPUs, GPUs, networking, and other components to work together efficiently. This creates an opportunity for AMD to benefit from the overall expansion in AI infrastructure, even if GPUs remain the primary engines for many AI workloads.
The opportunity surrounding CPUs could become particularly important as agentic AI applications require greater coordination between different computing resources.
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD)'s rapid expansion in AI has also raised expectations for the stock. The stock has gained more than 180% in 2026, reflecting investor optimism about the company's ability to capture a larger portion of the AI infrastructure market.
The stock trades at a premium, with a forward price-to-earnings multiple of 39X, roughly two times Nvidia's 19X. This means investors are paying considerably more for each dollar of AMD's expected future earnings.
Nevertheless, robust growth from a smaller base justifies AMD's valuation, as second-quarter revenue was up 50% while data center revenue more than doubled year over year. On the other hand, Nvidia boasts of a profitability advantage, as its gross margins stand at about 75% compared to AMD's 54%.
Any signs that AI infrastructure spending is slowing, or that AMD is capturing less of the expected CPU opportunity, could pressure investor sentiment. A significant portion of expected growth is also tied to hyperscalers, AI labs, and data-center infrastructure providers. If these customers reduce or delay capital expenditures, the company could experience a meaningful slowdown in growth.
Institutional investors have also been increasing their exposure to AMD amid the AI boom. As of the second quarter, 164 hedge funds held positions in AMD, up from 134 in the first quarter, indicating increased institutional participation.

Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD)'s investment story is increasingly tied to the broader AI computing ecosystem rather than GPUs alone. BofA's $720 price target reflects the firm's view that the rapid growth of AI workloads could create a substantial opportunity for AMD's EPYC CPUs alongside its Instinct GPUs and networking products.

Consider an illustrative cash-flow valuation. At the current equity value, $20 billion of sustainable annual free cash flow would imply about 50 times cash flow. The bearish route is that gaining accelerator share requires aggressive pricing, expensive engineering and customer support while the CPU business faces its own competition. Sales can rise substantially without free cash flow reaching the level the stock needs. The key disagreement is over profitable scale, not whether AMD can sell more chips.
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) has an operating foundation that can support accelerator development. At this price, the foundation must lead to much larger cash earnings. In late September 2016, Intel (INTC -0.56%) was worth about $177 billion. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +2.95%) was worth around $6.2 billion. Put another way, the chip giant's market value was about 28 times as big as its smaller rival's.
Ten years later, the order has flipped. AMD's market value is now around $1 trillion, while Intel's is about $622 billion, putting AMD about 60% ahead. AMD even announced a deal on Sept. 28 to buy artificial intelligence (AI) firm World Labs for about $8.2 billion in stock -- more than AMD's total market value a decade ago.
And that happened in a year when Intel shares have more than tripled as I write this. I think how AMD got here says plenty about what Intel's turnaround still needs to prove.
Image source: AMD.
In 2016, the two companies weren't in the same league. Intel reported revenue of $59.4 billion and operating income of $12.9 billion that year. AMD's revenue was $4.27 billion, and it had an operating loss of $372 million.
What's more, Intel's data center group alone pulled in $17.2 billion, around four times AMD's total sales.
AMD's comeback in servers took years. Mercury Research estimated AMD's share of x86 server processor units at just 3.2% in the fourth quarter of 2018. A year ago, AMD had around 27% of that market. The firm's latest numbers show it at 33.2% in the first quarter of 2026 and 34.5% in the second. So the gains keep coming, seven years after that low. And AMD's share of desktop processors rose from 15.8% to 34.9% in the same stretch.
Showing how far the balance has shifted, AMD's data center segment more than doubled its revenue year over year in the second quarter of 2026, to $6.7 billion. That beat the $6.3 billion for Intel's data center and AI segment, even though Intel's segment grew a strong 59%. Granted, AMD's number includes the graphics processing units it sells for AI, too.
And AMD is now earning more on less. Its second-quarter revenue climbed 50% year over year to $11.5 billion, and its operating income came in at $2.0 billion. Intel's operating income was $1.8 billion on $16.1 billion in revenue. Both swung from operating losses a year before.

Better chip designs arguably explain some of AMD's climb. But who made the chips might have mattered just as much.
AMD doesn't run its own factories. It released its second generation of EPYC server processors in August 2019, and it built them on what it called "leading-edge 7nm process technology." And in May, AMD said its latest server chips, code-named Venice, were ramping production on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's 2nm process.
Intel, though, makes chips at its own factories, so falling behind on manufacturing hurt its products directly. In July 2021, then-CEO Pat Gelsinger said Intel was speeding up its roadmap to get it on "a clear path to process performance leadership by 2025." Companies don't normally set that goal if they already hold the lead.
Can Intel's foundry win it back?
That history is why the foundry sits at the heart of Intel's turnaround. Its operating loss shrank to $2.1 billion in the second quarter of 2026, from $2.4 billion in the first quarter and $3.2 billion a year before. Revenue grew 31% year over year to $5.8 billion.
But nearly all of that revenue is from Intel itself. Outside customers brought in $293 million of it in the second quarter, around 5% of the total.

Intel has committed to finishing its next process, 14A. Its second-quarter 10-Q also says the size and speed of its manufacturing build-out will "ultimately be dictated by the amount of committed demand for Intel 14A" -- including from outside customers.
Winning that demand probably takes convincing chip designers like AMD that Intel can make their most advanced products as well as Taiwan Semiconductor can. It's the ground Intel lost, and I'd say the turnaround isn't done until Intel wins some of it back.
True, Intel's business is improving. Its operating income swung to a profit in the second quarter, and the foundry's losses are shrinking. But at around 57 times its expected 2027 earnings, Intel stock is pricier than AMD, the company that overtook it, at about 40 times its expected 2027 earnings.
I think Intel's share price already assumes a lot of that ground has been won back. For now, outside customers still make up around 5% of the foundry's revenue.

Shares of Advanced Micro Devices climbed 2% during Friday’s trading session after the semiconductor manufacturer revealed its latest AI integration developed in partnership with Perplexity. The collaboration focuses on bringing Perplexity’s Portable Computer functionality to Windows-based systems equipped with AMD’s Ryzen AI Max processors, including devices running the Ryzen AI Halo developer platform.
This functionality enables users to perform AI operations entirely on their local hardware. By processing tasks on-device, users can establish automated workflows without depleting their allocation of Perplexity Computer credits used for cloud-based inference.

Perplexity contributes its AI model infrastructure and agent technologies to the partnership. The combined offering aims to transform agentic PCs from a specialized novelty into a mainstream computing option.
The strategic importance of this announcement extends beyond the immediate technology. While cloud-based AI processing currently dominates the market, AMD is positioning itself for a potential shift toward local AI execution as user demand evolves.

Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)’s Halo Station Could Strengthen Its AI Position, but Near-Term Revenue Impact May Be Limited
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc (NASDAQ:AMD) has set its sights on capitalizing on the growing demand for workstations capable of running large artificial intelligence models. On September 4, the company unveiled the Threadripper Halo Station, expanding its AI strategy beyond data centers and into high-end local AI computing.
Designed for AI development and inference, the AI-powered workstation is capable of running AI models with more than one trillion parameters locally and offers up to 16.4 TB/s of total system memory bandwidth. Consequently, it is well-suited for AI teams and researchers working on highly sensitive workloads.
The new Halo Station creates a potential new market for AMD between conventional PCs and data center servers. Therefore, it allows the company to move beyond simply selling CPUs by combining Threadripper Pro processors, high-capacity memory, and Instinct AI accelerators in a single workstation platform.
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc (AMD)’s Halo Station Could Strengthen Its AI Position, but Revenue Impact Is Years Away
The new AI work station positions AMD to take on Nvidia's DGX Station systems. More importantly, broader adoption of Instinct-based workstations could help AMD expand its ROCm software ecosystem, which remains critical to narrowing Nvidia's longstanding advantage with CUDA.
The workstation could therefore serve as more than a hardware product. If developers increasingly use Instinct accelerators for local AI development and inference, AMD could gain an opportunity to expand its software ecosystem and encourage developers to build applications around its hardware. This could strengthen the company's broader competitive position in AI infrastructure.
However, the Halo Station also faces significant challenges. Hardware specifications alone are unlikely to be enough for Advanced Micro Devices, Inc (NASDAQ:AMD) to seriously challenge Nvidia. Developers typically require a mature software environment, including optimized libraries, frameworks, developer tools, and applications. Nvidia's CUDA ecosystem benefits from years of developer adoption and remains a formidable competitive moat.
Cost is another potential obstacle. AMD has not disclosed pricing, but the Halo Station's high-end Threadripper Pro and Instinct configuration suggests it will primarily target AI researchers, developers, and specialized enterprise workloads rather than mainstream PC buyers.
Timing presents another consideration. The Halo Station is expected to launch in 2027, meaning investors may have to wait before the product has a meaningful impact on AMD's financial results. While the workstation could become an important component of AMD's broader AI strategy, it is too early to assume that it will develop into a major standalone revenue stream.
Hedge Fund Positioning and Short Interest
As Advanced Micro Devices, Inc (NASDAQ:AMD) continues to explore new growth opportunities around AI, institutional positioning has also been building. The number of hedge funds holding stakes in the company grew to 164 in the second quarter from 134 in the first quarter, according to the Insider Monkey Database. Marshall Wace is one of the institutional investors that hiked its stake in the company by 3% to $2.26 billion, even as DE Shaw cut its stake by 21% to $1.79 billion.
On the other hand, bearish positioning around AMD is small, with 2.46% short interest as of August 14, representing 40.1 million shares sold short.
The Threadripper Halo Station gives Advanced Micro Devices, Inc (NASDAQ:AMD) another avenue to capitalize on the expanding AI infrastructure market. More importantly, wider workstation adoption could help it strengthen the ROCm ecosystem and gradually reduce Nvidia's software advantage.
However, investors should view the Halo Station as a long-term strategic opportunity rather than an immediate revenue catalyst. Its potentially high price, niche target market, 2027 launch timeline, and AMD's ongoing software disadvantage against Nvidia's CUDA ecosystem all represent meaningful risks.

As the artificial intelligence boom matures, choosing between high-growth processors and steady analog chips requires a careful look at Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +2.95%) and Texas Instruments (TXN +4.44%) as potential long-term investments.
Advanced Micro Devices focuses on high-performance computing for data centers and gaming, while Texas Instruments dominates the analog world with chips for industrial and automotive uses. While both operate in the same broad category, their business models and growth profiles offer very different opportunities for retail investors today.
Advanced Micro Devices designs processors and graphics chips for everything from laptops to massive data centers. Key partnerships include a strategic agreement with OpenAI to deploy advanced graphics units, alongside long-term deals with Sony (SONY +1.41%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) for gaming hardware. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business since a few large buyers drive much of the volume.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $34.6 billion, an increase of 34% over the prior year. Net income was roughly $4.3 billion, and AMD reported a net margin of approximately 12.5% for the year. This upward trend highlights the strong demand for the company's newest products among semiconductor stocks.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1, indicating that AMD relies very little on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to pay short-term debts with current assets, is roughly 2.9. Free cash flow reached nearly $6.7 billion, though note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 21.2% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Texas Instruments offers a massive catalog of more than 80,000 products, focusing on analog and embedded processing. The company serves over 100,000 customers globally, primarily in the industrial and automotive markets. Because the customer base is highly diverse, with roughly half of total revenue generated by customers outside of its largest 50, the company does not rely heavily on any single buyer.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $17.7 billion, up 13% compared to the previous year. Net income was $5 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 28%. In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, Texas Instruments highlighted its focus on making electronics more affordable through its manufacturing scale.
Based on the December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is close to 0.9. The current ratio is approximately 4.4, suggesting the company maintains a strong cushion for its immediate financial obligations. Free cash flow for the year was nearly $2.6 billion, providing capital to support its long-term manufacturing expansion and return value to shareholders.
Advanced Micro Devices faces intense competition from Intel (INTC -0.56%) and Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%), especially following strategic partnerships between those rivals. Geopolitical risks are also present, as U.S. export controls on advanced chips to China have caused inventory charges. Additionally, the company relies heavily on TSMC (TSM +2.96%) for manufacturing and must navigate the integration of recent acquisitions like ZT Systems.
Texas Instruments must manage the cyclical nature of the chip industry, which often sees volatile demand. Because the company owns its manufacturing plants, it faces high fixed costs that are difficult to reduce during market downturns. Significant revenue comes from customers in China, making it vulnerable to trade barriers. TI is also currently in the middle of acquiring Silicon Laboratories (SLAB +0.11%).
Advanced Micro Devices trades at a significantly higher premium than Texas Instruments when comparing the forward P/E and P/S ratio metrics.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Presumably, investors are paying a premium for AMD because of its strong revenue growth (Texas Instruments' growth didn't come close to AMD's last fiscal year). That said, I am more interested in each company's net margin. Using fiscal 2025 figures, TI's margin pretty handily tops AMD's full-year results. And while both companies have seen profits expand by a few percentage points over the trailing 12 months, that profitability gap has continued into this fiscal year.
As far as their actual business models, I do think AMD's fabless approach is more attractive, because it gives the company more flexibility. Texas Instruments, conversely, has to deal with the high fixed costs of owning and running its manufacturing plants.
AMD stock has absolutely exploded over the past 10 years, while Texas Instruments shares have modestly outperformed the S&P 500 over that same time frame. Past performance is no indication of future results, but it's worth taking into consideration.
All told, I like Texas Instruments better here because it appeals to the conservative side of me: It’s not crazy expensive, it has stronger profitability, and it pays a dividend yielding just over 2.1%.

In FY 2025, Qualcomm's revenue reached $44.3 billion, a roughly 13.7% increase over the $39.0 billion reported in FY 2024. Net income for the period, however, fell sharply to $5.5 billion, down about 45% from the $10.1 billion reported in FY 2024, resulting in a net margin of nearly 12.5%, despite the strong top-line growth. The drop in net income wasn't due to weak operations or R&D costs; it was mainly a one-time, non-cash $5.7 billion charge tied to the U.S. government's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Excluding that charge, Qualcomm's underlying profits actually grew nicely.
As of its September 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio stands at roughly 2.8x, indicating the company has sufficient short-term assets to cover its obligations. The debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.7x, showing a higher level of leverage compared to some peers in the industry. Free cash flow for the fiscal year was nearly $12.8 billion, which is the cash left over after a company pays for its capital expenditures from its operating cash flow.
Advanced Micro Devices faces intense competition from Intel (INTC -0.56%) and Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%), both of which leverage large software ecosystems to maintain market share. Geopolitical tensions also pose a threat, as evidenced by an $800 million inventory charge in early 2025 due to U.S. export controls on sales to China. Additionally, the company relies heavily on third-party foundries like TSMC, making it vulnerable to any manufacturing disruptions or capacity shortages.
Qualcomm deals with significant revenue concentration among a few mobile handset manufacturers, many of whom are increasingly developing their own internal chips. The company also remains highly exposed to regulatory and trade policy risks involving China, which serves as a critical manufacturing hub. Furthermore, ongoing legal challenges to its patent licensing model could fundamentally alter its high-margin revenue streams if future court rulings are unfavorable.
Qualcomm currently trades at a much lower Forward P/E and P/S ratio than AMD, suggesting a more conservative valuation of its future earnings estimates.
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with AMD, although Qualcomm's ongoing transformation beyond smartphones is worth acknowledging. Its automotive segment just posted a record quarter, growing at an extraordinary rate year over year. A new partnership with BMW cements its position as a key player in next-generation vehicles, and an emerging data center business adds another growth engine that could matter a great deal in the years ahead.
But Qualcomm is also navigating a difficult stretch in its core smartphone business. Android handset demand is soft, and memory cost increases are squeezing margins. A sharp drop in Apple revenue is expected in the coming quarter. Those headwinds are manageable but create near-term uncertainty that concerns me.
The path forward at AMD is considerably cleaner. Data center sales more than doubled year over year. A partnership with Anthropic backs up management's confidence in continued growth, and the company keeps posting results that surprise analysts to the upside. For a long-term investor, AMD's remarkable momentum in the most important part of the semiconductor market makes it the stronger pick right now.

This creates an opportunity for AMD to benefit from the overall expansion in AI infrastructure, even if GPUs remain the primary engines for many AI workloads.
The opportunity surrounding CPUs could become particularly important as agentic AI applications require greater coordination between different computing resources.
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.’s rapid expansion in AI has also raised expectations for the stock. The stock has gained more than 180% in 2026, reflecting investor optimism about the company’s ability to capture a larger portion of the AI infrastructure market.

In late September 2016, Intel (INTC -0.56%) was worth about $177 billion. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +2.95%) was worth around $6.2 billion. Put another way, the chip giant's market value was about 28 times as big as its smaller rival's.

Better chip designs arguably explain some of AMD's climb. But who made the chips might have mattered just as much.

In July 2021, then-CEO Pat Gelsinger said Intel was speeding up its roadmap to get it on "a clear path to process performance leadership by 2025." Companies don't normally set that goal if they already hold the lead.
Can Intel's foundry win it back?
That history is why the foundry sits at the heart of Intel's turnaround. Its operating loss shrank to $2.1 billion in the second quarter of 2026, from $2.4 billion in the first quarter and $3.2 billion a year before. Revenue grew 31% year over year to $5.8 billion.
